Don't.
Slide it.
One number leaves, one enters.
Again.
New best.

Every number enters once and leaves
once.
That's linear time, and it's the trick
behind half the substring questions
you'll see.

clips.transcript: Find the biggest sum of three numbers in a row. Most people re-add every window. Don't. Slide it. One number leaves, one enters. 8 − 2 + 1 = 7. Again. 7 − 1 + 3 = 9. New best. Last slide gives 6. The answer is 9. Every number enters once and leaves once. That's linear time, and it's the trick behind half the substring questions you'll see.

fraud that really happened, how much did
it catch?
That's recall.
When positives are rare, accuracy mostly
measures how common normal is.
Look at recall, precision, and the
precision-recall curve.

clips.transcript: This model is 99% accurate. It has never caught a single fraud. Here's why. A hundred transactions. One of them is fraud. The model just says “normal” every time. 99 right, 1 wrong. 99%. Now ask the better question: of the fraud that really happened, how much did it catch? 0%. That's recall. When positives are rare, accuracy mostly measures how common normal is. Look at recall, precision, and the precision-recall curve.

clips.headline: The internet's first word was “LO”

follow.title: The internet's first message
follow.body: At about 10:30 p.m. on October 29, 1969, UCLA student programmer Charley Kline, supervised by Professor Leonard Kleinrock, tried to log in from UCLA's SDS Sigma 7 to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over ARPANET. The L and the O arrived; the system crashed before the G. The full login went through about an hour later.

cues.t: The first message ever sent over the
network that became the internet was two
letters long.
A UCLA student, Charley Kline, tries to
log in to a computer at Stanford
Research Institute.
L.
O.
G.
And the system crashes.
So the first word on the internet was
“lo.” As in, lo and behold.
About an hour later, the full login went
through.

clips.transcript: The first message ever sent over the network that became the internet was two letters long. Oct 29, 1969. A UCLA student, Charley Kline, tries to log in to a computer at Stanford Research Institute. L. O. G. And the system crashes. So the first word on the internet was “lo.” As in, lo and behold. About an hour later, the full login went through.

clips.headline: O 14-Bis e os 220 metros de 1906

follow.title: Santos Dumont e o 14-Bis
follow.body: Em 23 de outubro de 1906, no Campo de Bagatelle, em Paris, Alberto Santos Dumont voou cerca de 60 metros com o 14-Bis e ganhou a taça Archdeacon. Em 12 de novembro, voou 220 metros em cerca de 21 segundos, o primeiro voo motorizado reconhecido oficialmente na Europa.
follow.source: Britannica; U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission
